questions.prompt: You precompute prefix[i] = sum of nums[0..i-1] (so prefix has length n+1). Which expression gives the sum of nums[l..r] inclusive?
questions.explanation: prefix[r + 1] holds nums[0..r] and prefix[l] holds nums[0..l-1]. Subtracting removes everything before l, leaving nums[l..r]. The extra leading 0 slot avoids a special case for l = 0.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of inserting an element at index n/2 of a Java ArrayList holding n elements (capacity is sufficient)?
questions.explanation: Every element after the insertion point must shift one slot right (System.arraycopy), which is about n/2 moves, so O(n). Only appends at the end are amortised O(1).

questions.prompt: Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum subarray sum in O(n). At each index, what does it decide?
options: Whether to sort the remaining elements
Whether to extend the best subarray ending at the previous index or start fresh at the current element
Whether the current element is larger than the global maximum
Whether to binary search for the next positive number
questions.explanation: bestEndingHere = max(nums[i], bestEndingHere + nums[i]). Starting fresh is better when the running sum has gone negative. The global answer is the max of bestEndingHere over all i.

questions.prompt: For 'product of array except self' without division, which approach gives O(n) time and O(1) extra space (excluding the output array)?
options: Nested loops multiplying all other elements
Sort the array, then multiply neighbours
Fill the output with prefix products left-to-right, then multiply in suffix products right-to-left with a running variable
Use a hash map from value to product
questions.explanation: output[i] first holds the product of everything to the left of i. A second pass from the right multiplies in a running product of everything to the right. Only one extra scalar is needed.

questions.prompt: Why is building a large string with s = s + piece inside a loop slow in Java?
options: String concatenation is not allowed in loops
Strings are immutable, so each + creates a new String and copies the existing characters, giving O(n^2) total work
The JVM disables the string pool inside loops
questions.explanation: Each iteration allocates a new String and copies everything built so far. A StringBuilder appends into a growable buffer, giving amortised O(n) total.

questions.prompt: What is the most efficient way to check whether two lowercase ASCII strings of length n are anagrams?
options: Generate all permutations of one string
Sort both strings and compare: O(n log n)
Count characters with an int[26] array: O(n)
questions.explanation: Increment counts for one string and decrement for the other; they are anagrams if every count ends at zero. Sorting also works but is O(n log n). Equal hashCodes do not imply equal contents.

questions.prompt: Using 'expand around centre' to find the longest palindromic substring, how many centres must be checked in a string of length n?
questions.explanation: Odd-length palindromes centre on a character (n centres) and even-length ones centre between two characters (n - 1 centres), so 2n - 1 in total. Each expansion is O(n), giving O(n^2) overall with O(1) space.

questions.prompt: Two Sum: find indices i != j with nums[i] + nums[j] == target. What does the standard one-pass HashMap solution store?
options: Each index mapped to its value
Each value seen so far mapped to its index; for every element check whether target - value is already present
Every pair sum mapped to its two indices
Only the values that are below target
questions.explanation: Looking up the complement before inserting the current value guarantees i != j and finds the pair in a single O(n) pass.

questions.prompt: Since Java 8, what is the worst-case lookup time in a HashMap bucket that holds many colliding keys which implement Comparable?
options: O(log n), because large buckets are converted into red-black trees
questions.explanation: When a bucket exceeds TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8) and the table has at least 64 slots, the bucket becomes a balanced tree, bounding lookups at O(log n). Without treeification a degenerate bucket is a linked list and lookups are O(n).

questions.prompt: To find the longest run of consecutive integers in an unsorted array in O(n), you put all values in a HashSet. Which values do you start counting from?
options: Only values v where v - 1 is not in the set
questions.explanation: Starting only at sequence beginnings means each number is visited a constant number of times overall, so the total is O(n) even though there is an inner while loop.

questions.prompt: In a sorted array, you look for a pair summing to target with pointers at both ends. If nums[left] + nums[right] < target, what should you do?
questions.explanation: The sum is too small. Because the array is sorted, moving left rightwards is the only move that can increase the sum.

questions.prompt: In 'Container With Most Water', why is it safe to move the pointer at the shorter line inward?
options: Because the shorter line will be reused later
Because any container using the shorter line with a closer partner is narrower and still capped by that short height, so it can't be larger
Because the taller line is always part of the answer
It isn't safe; you must try both moves
questions.explanation: Area = min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l). Keeping the shorter line while shrinking the width can never beat the current area, so that line can be discarded.

questions.prompt: To remove duplicates in-place from a sorted array, a slow pointer marks the write position. When does the fast pointer's value get written?
options: When it differs from the last written value
When it is larger than the first element
questions.explanation: Sorted order puts equal values next to each other, so comparing with the last kept value is enough. The result is O(n) time with O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: For the longest substring without repeating characters, what happens when the right pointer reaches a character already inside the window?
options: Move the left pointer past the previous occurrence of that character
Move the right pointer back one
questions.explanation: Storing each character's last index lets left jump to max(left, lastIndex + 1). Each pointer only moves forward, so the algorithm is O(n).

questions.prompt: To compute every average of a fixed window of size k, how do you update the window sum when sliding by one?
options: Recompute the sum of all k elements
Add the entering element and subtract the leaving element
questions.explanation: This is O(1) per step and O(n) overall, instead of O(nk) from recomputing each window.

questions.prompt: Why does the classic variable sliding window fail for 'shortest subarray with sum >= k' when the array contains negative numbers?
options: Shrinking the window no longer reliably decreases the sum, so monotonic window movement is invalid
Hash maps can't store negative keys
questions.explanation: The two-pointer window relies on sums changing monotonically as it grows or shrinks. With negatives you need prefix sums plus a monotonic deque (an O(n) solution) instead.

questions.prompt: Why do many implementations write mid = low + (high - low) / 2 instead of (low + high) / 2?
options: It avoids int overflow when low + high exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE
It rounds up instead of down
questions.explanation: low + high can overflow to a negative value for large indices. (low + high) >>> 1 is another overflow-safe option in Java.

questions.prompt: When searching a rotated sorted array (distinct values), what can you always conclude after computing mid?
options: At least one of the halves [low..mid] or [mid..high] is sorted
The target is in the right half
questions.explanation: Comparing nums[low] with nums[mid] tells you which half is sorted. Check whether the target lies inside that sorted half's range and discard the other half. Each step is O(1), so the search is O(log n).

questions.prompt: 'Minimum ship capacity to deliver all packages within D days' is solved with binary search over what?
options: The capacity values, using a greedy check of whether a capacity finishes within D days
questions.explanation: Feasibility is monotonic: if capacity c works, every larger capacity works too. Search between max(weight) and sum(weights) with an O(n) greedy check, giving O(n log(sum)).

questions.prompt: Floyd's cycle detection moves a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps. What indicates a cycle?
options: The slow pointer reaches the head again
questions.explanation: Inside a cycle the fast pointer closes the gap by one node per step, so they must meet. If fast reaches null there is no cycle. It uses O(1) space.

questions.prompt: Iteratively reversing a singly linked list needs which pointers?
questions.explanation: Save next, point current.next at prev, then advance prev and current. It runs in O(n) time with O(1) space.

questions.prompt: Why do many linked-list solutions (merge two lists, remove nth from end) start with a dummy/sentinel node?
options: To make the list doubly linked
To remove special-case handling when the head itself changes or is removed
questions.explanation: With dummy.next = head, every real node, including the head, has a predecessor, so insertions and deletions follow one uniform code path. Return dummy.next at the end.

questions.prompt: Checking balanced brackets like "({[]})", what does a stack-based solution do on a closing bracket?
options: Pop and verify the popped opener matches; fail if the stack is empty or mismatched
questions.explanation: The string is valid only if every closer matches the most recent unmatched opener and the stack is empty at the end.

questions.prompt: To find the next greater element for every index in O(n), which structure is used?
options: A monotonic decreasing stack of indices
questions.explanation: When the current value is greater than the value at the stack's top index, it is that index's next greater element: pop it and record the answer. Each index is pushed and popped at most once.

questions.prompt: In modern Java, which is generally the recommended implementation for a stack or queue?
questions.explanation: ArrayDeque is a resizable circular array with no synchronization overhead. Its Javadoc notes it is likely faster than Stack used as a stack and faster than LinkedList used as a queue. Stack extends the synchronized Vector.

questions.prompt: What does an in-order traversal of a binary search tree produce?
questions.explanation: In-order visits left subtree, node, right subtree. In a BST everything on the left is smaller and everything on the right is larger, so the output is sorted.

questions.prompt: Why is checking node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val at every node NOT enough to validate a BST?
options: A deeper descendant can violate an ancestor's bound, so you must pass (min, max) bounds down the recursion
questions.explanation: Example: root 5, left child 3, and 3's right child 6. Each parent-child pair looks fine, but 6 sits in 5's left subtree. Pass inclusive or exclusive bounds down (use long or nullable bounds to avoid edge cases).

questions.prompt: Which traversal naturally produces a tree's nodes level by level?
questions.explanation: BFS processes nodes in order of distance from the root. Reading queue.size() at the start of each iteration separates the levels.

questions.prompt: In a BST, how do you find the lowest common ancestor of p and q efficiently?
options: Store both root-to-node paths and compare every node
From the root, go left if both are smaller, right if both are larger; otherwise the current node is the LCA
questions.explanation: The first node where p and q split to different sides (or that equals one of them) is the LCA. It takes O(h) time, where h is the tree height.

questions.prompt: To find the k largest elements of a stream of n numbers with O(k) memory, which heap do you keep?
options: A min-heap of size k, evicting the smallest when it grows beyond k
No heap; sort at the end
questions.explanation: The min-heap's root is the smallest of the current top k, so it is the one to evict when a bigger value arrives. This is O(n log k).

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from n unsorted elements using bottom-up heapify (sift-down from the last parent)?
questions.explanation: Most nodes are near the bottom and sift only a short distance. Summing the heights gives a convergent series, so the total is O(n). Inserting elements one by one is O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Iterating over a java.util.PriorityQueue with a for-each loop yields elements in what order?
options: No guaranteed order; only poll() returns elements in priority order
questions.explanation: The iterator walks the backing array, which is only heap-ordered. Use repeated poll(), or copy and sort, to get sorted output.

questions.prompt: In an unweighted graph, which algorithm finds the shortest path (fewest edges) from a source?
questions.explanation: BFS explores nodes in increasing distance order, so the first time a node is reached is via a shortest path. It runs in O(V + E).

questions.prompt: Why is Dijkstra's algorithm incorrect with negative edge weights?
options: It finalises a node when it is popped, assuming no later path can be cheaper; a negative edge can break that assumption
questions.explanation: Use Bellman-Ford (O(VE)) when negative weights exist. It can also detect negative cycles.

questions.prompt: Using Kahn's algorithm for topological sort, how do you detect a cycle?
options: The output contains fewer nodes than the graph
questions.explanation: Nodes on a cycle never reach in-degree 0, so they never enter the queue. If the processed count is less than V, there is a cycle (for example, a course schedule that can't be completed).

questions.prompt: With both path compression and union by rank, what is the amortised cost per Union-Find operation?
options: O(alpha(n)), the inverse Ackermann function, which is effectively constant
questions.explanation: This is Tarjan's classic result. alpha(n) is at most 4 for any realistic n. Union-Find is ideal for connectivity and Kruskal's MST.

questions.prompt: How many subsets does a set of n distinct elements have?
questions.explanation: Each element is either in or out of the subset, giving 2^n. Backtracking over subsets therefore takes at least O(n * 2^n) to output them all.

questions.prompt: In a backtracking solution that builds a path in a shared list, what must happen after the recursive call returns?
options: Undo the choice (remove the last element) so the next branch starts from the correct state
questions.explanation: Choose, explore, un-choose. When recording a result, copy the list (new ArrayList<>(path)); otherwise later mutations change the stored result.

questions.prompt: In N-Queens, which bookkeeping lets you check whether a square is attacked in O(1)?
options: Sets (or boolean arrays) of used columns, used (row - col) diagonals and used (row + col) anti-diagonals
Only a set of used rows
questions.explanation: Placing one queen per row handles rows. Cells on the same diagonal share row - col, and cells on the same anti-diagonal share row + col.

questions.prompt: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. What recurrence gives ways(n)?
questions.explanation: The last move was either a 1-step from n-1 or a 2-step from n-2. That is the Fibonacci recurrence, computable in O(n) time and O(1) space.

questions.prompt: Minimum coins to make amount A (unlimited coins). What is dp[a]?
options: The number of ways to make a
min over coins c <= a of dp[a - c] + 1, with dp[0] = 0
questions.explanation: This is O(A * coins). Greedy (always take the largest coin) fails for some coin systems, e.g. coins {1, 3, 4} with amount 6: greedy gives 4+1+1, but 3+3 is optimal.

questions.prompt: For longest common subsequence of strings a and b, what is dp[i][j] when a[i-1] == b[j-1]?
questions.explanation: Matching characters extend the LCS of the two prefixes. Otherwise take max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). This is O(mn) time, and space can be reduced to O(min(m, n)).

questions.prompt: Using a 1-D array for 0/1 knapsack, why must the capacity loop run from high to low?
options: Iterating downward ensures each item is used at most once, because dp[w - weight] still holds the previous item's row
questions.explanation: Iterating upward would read values already updated for the current item, effectively allowing unlimited copies. That is the unbounded knapsack.

questions.prompt: To select the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals, which greedy rule is optimal?
options: Sort by end time and repeatedly take the interval that ends earliest and doesn't overlap
Sort by start time and take the earliest start
Pick intervals with the fewest overlaps
questions.explanation: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the remaining intervals. An exchange argument shows it is never worse than an optimal solution.

questions.prompt: Jump Game (can you reach the last index?) can be solved greedily by tracking what?
options: The furthest index reachable so far; fail if the current index ever exceeds it
A DP table of size n^2
questions.explanation: It is a single O(n) pass: reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]). If i > reach at any point, the end is unreachable.
